conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how things have been feeling for you since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. It’s simply 10 questions about your mood, thoughts, and well-being over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; whatever you share stays between us unless safety is a concern, and then we’ll make a plan together. When you’re ready, we’ll go through each question—I’ll re-phrase them in everyday language so they feel less clinical. Ready to start?

In the past week, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not very much… I can still laugh if something’s genuinely hilarious—like yesterday my husband made a silly face when he spilled the coffee—but it feels muted. Most of the day I’m too tired or worried to find much funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I guess I’d say “not so much.” I can still chuckle once in a while, but it’s like the joy is turned way down—most things just feel flat or I’m too worn-out to care.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Not really… even little things I used to like—watching my show or getting coffee—feel kind of “meh.” I’ll still do them, but the excitement isn’t there; it’s more like I’m going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah, I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not a good enough mom. Even when my husband says it’s normal, I still feel it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll lie there after a feeding and my mind just races—what if he stops breathing, what if I drop him, what if I’m missing something? Nothing’s actually happening, but I can’t shut the thoughts off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Yes—maybe three or four times this week. My heart starts pounding and I get this tight-chest feeling, like something awful is about to happen, even when the baby’s asleep and the house is quiet.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly feel like the pile is endless, like I’m drowning in little tasks. Sometimes I have to set the baby in the crib for a minute, step into the hallway, and just breathe so I don’t burst into tears.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. I’ll finally get the baby down, but then I lie there with my mind spinning—going over everything I might’ve done wrong, worrying something bad will happen—and it takes me forever to fall asleep. Even when I do drift off, I jerk awake at least once or twice with the same anxious thoughts.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s not tears-all-day awful, but there’s this heavy, gray feeling that just sits on me. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel like I could cry for no real reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Once was after a night when the baby wouldn’t settle and I just felt like I was failing him; I ended up sobbing in the bathroom so no one would hear.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

A couple of times, when everything feels too heavy, I’ll get this quick flash—like “what if I just weren’t here?”—but I’ve never planned anything and I don’t want to leave my baby. It’s more a passing, scary thought I try to push away.

You've shared that the past week has felt overwhelmingly heavy: joy seems muted, daily tasks feel like drowning, and a gray mood hangs over even the sweet moments with your baby. You're exhausted yet lie awake with racing "what-if" thoughts, blame yourself whenever your little one fusses, and have had a few sudden waves of panic or tearfulness. You mentioned fleeting scary thoughts of not being here, though you quickly push them away and emphatically want to stay with your child. These feelings are understandably frightening and draining, and reaching out is a strong, courageous step.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports noticeably reduced ability to laugh/feel joy, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost no enjoyment or anticipation, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('I do that a lot') and attributes baby's distress entirely to her perceived maternal failure, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive racing thoughts with no external trigger, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple clear panic episodes with physical symptoms and dread, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm and inability to manage routine tasks, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption due to persistent anxious/ruminative thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "pretty much every day" and spontaneous crying, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying twice this week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score ≥14 and item 10 ≥1 indicate high likelihood of major <med>postpartum depression</med> with comorbid <med>anxiety</med>. You endorse <sym>depressed mood</sym> most of the time, markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), <sym>self-reproach</sym>, <sym>sleep disruption</sym> beyond infant care needs, <sym>feelings of inadequacy</sym>, recurrent panic-type symptoms, and passive <sym>suicidal ideation</sym> without intent. This pattern meets screening criteria consistent with <med>DSM-5 Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> to review results and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> and evidence-based therapies such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med>
3. Consider whether <med>antidepressant medication</med> or other pharmacologic support is appropriate for you
4. Identify trusted support persons who can help with overnight infant care so you can obtain 4-5 hours of uninterrupted sleep
5. Plan daily 10-15 minute outdoor walks or gentle movement; sunlight and activity aid mood and <sym>anxiety</sym> reduction
6. Use brief mindfulness or breathing apps when <sym>panic sensations</sym> arise; practice inhale 4 sec, hold 2, exhale 6
7. Create a safety plan: list 24/7 hotlines (<med>988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline</med>, <med>Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773</med>) and local emergency numbers
8. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2-3 weeks to monitor progress once treatment begins
9. Reassure yourself: these symptoms are common, treatable, and not a reflection of your love or capability as a mother
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

Patient: Postpartum parent (infant approx. 2–3 wks old)  
Date: ___  
Clinician: ___

Symptoms endorsed:
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt re parenting adequacy  
- Marked anxiety (racing thoughts, “what-if” worries), 3–4 panic-equivalent episodes this week  
- Sleep disturbance driven by intrusive worries even when infant settled  
- Feeling overwhelmed/drowning in routine tasks; daily emotional exhaustion  
- Passive suicidal ideation (fleeting thoughts “not being here”) without plan or intent

Pattern: Symptoms present daily for past week, interfere with functioning and enjoyment of infant.  
Highest-risk items: Q8, Q9, Q10 → warrant safety review.

Screening impression: High likelihood of major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; active safety concern (passive SI) requires immediate risk assessment and follow-up.
